definition: Starship's first stage. In Block 3 it is about 72 m tall, powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, and designed to be caught by the launch tower and reflown.
The upper stage and spacecraft. Block 3 ships carry three sea-level Raptors and three Raptor Vacuum engines, a hexagonal-tile heat shield and four flaps for atmospheric control.
SpaceX's full-flow staged-combustion engine burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Raptor 3 integrates most plumbing internally and needs no heat shield around its exterior.
A Raptor with a large nozzle extension optimised for vacuum. RVacs are fixed (not gimbaled) and provide most of the ship's ascent thrust above the atmosphere.
The point of maximum dynamic pressure: the combination of air density and speed that puts the greatest aerodynamic stress on the vehicle, usually about a minute after liftoff.
Shutdown of most of Super Heavy's engines just before stage separation.
Shutdown of the ship's engines at the end of the ascent burn.
Separation technique in which the ship lights its engines while still attached to the booster. Exhaust escapes through the vented interstage, and the extra push improves performance.
After separation, Super Heavy flips and burns its engines to reverse course back toward the launch site or a landing zone in the Gulf.
Final engine burn that slows a stage to near zero velocity for a tower catch or a soft splashdown.
The two mechanical arms on the launch tower (Mechazilla) that stack vehicles and catch returning boosters and ships out of the air.
The structure Super Heavy sits on before launch, with hold-down clamps, the quick-disconnects that load propellant, and the flame deflector.
A water-cooled steel plate under the launch mount that sprays water during ignition to protect the pad and suppress the noise of 33 Raptors.
Lattice-shaped control surfaces at the top of Super Heavy that steer it during descent. On Block 3 there are three larger fins.
The ship's four movable control surfaces (two forward, two aft) used to steer the 'skydiver' belly-first descent.
Starship's horizontal, belly-first fall through the lower atmosphere, which maximises drag before the landing flip.
The rapid rotation from horizontal to vertical just before landing, while the engines relight for the landing burn.
The altitude, around 100–120 km, where reentry heating begins to matter.
Communication loss caused by ionised gas around the vehicle during peak heating. Starlink links through the plasma wake largely keep contact on Starship flights.
Thousands of hexagonal ceramic tiles covering the ship's windward side to survive temperatures above 1,400 °C during reentry.
A short burn that raises the perigee of the ship's path above the atmosphere, turning a suborbital trajectory into a stable orbit.
A retrograde burn that lowers the perigee into the atmosphere so the ship reenters at a planned location.
The lowest and highest points of an orbit above Earth.
The angle between the orbital plane and the equator. Launching due east from Starbase (26° N) gives about 26°. Flight 14 flew at 30.5°.
The slot in the ship's payload bay through which Starlink satellites are pushed out one at a time, named after the candy dispenser.
The third-generation Starlink satellite, sized for Starship. Each one adds far more capacity than the V2 Mini satellites launched on Falcon 9.
Moving cryogenic propellant between two Starships in orbit. This is key to refuelling for lunar and Mars missions.
A ground test that fires the engines while the vehicle is clamped down, done before every flight.
A full propellant load and countdown rehearsal that stops before ignition.
Generations of Starship hardware. Block 3 (V3) brings Raptor 3, stretched tanks and a new hot-stage ring, and is designed for orbital operations, propellant transfer and full reuse.
Speeds around Mach 1, where airflow is partly subsonic and partly supersonic, with large aerodynamic changes.
Live data streamed from the vehicle, such as speed, altitude, propellant levels and engine status, shown on the webcast overlay.
